title: India’s fintech ecosystem needs to move from financial access to investor outcomes, experts say- Moneycontrol.com
text:
My Alerts Go Ad-Free Follow us on: As digital public infrastructure expands access to financial products, experts say the next phase should focus on better financial advice, data portability and helping households achieve their financial goals.   September 11, 2026 / 09:02 IST             India’s fintech ecosystem needs to move beyond expanding access to financial products and focus on whether investors are actually achieving their financial goals, experts said at the Global Fintech Fest on September 10. India’s digital public infrastructure has enabled financial services to reach the population at unprecedented scale. More than 1 billion Aadhaar-linked identities, over 14 billion monthly UPI transactions and around 100 million Account Aggregator-linked profiles have helped expand access to the financial system, said Smita Jha, Partner, Banking and Finance, Khaitan & Co., who moderated the panel. But the next challenge is to ensure that access translates into better financial decisions and outcomes, speakers said during a session on building India’s financial advice stack as part of the digital public infrastructure. More products do not necessarily mean better outcomes Jeet Ketan Marwadi, Founder & Managing Director, 1 Finance said rapid digitisation has enabled people to access and accumulate financial products, but many investors continue to look at their finances in silos. Mutual fund folios have grown threefold over the past five years to around six crore individual investors, he said. However, accumulating financial products does not necessarily mean that households are moving closer to their financial goals. Investors often look at mutual funds, insurance,  loans,   real estate and other assets separately rather than considering their entire financial position, Marwadi said. “The biggest challenge for that is that people are looking at their entire financial picture in silos and focusing too much on investing rather than cash flow management, rather than liability management, rather than looking at their real estate portfolio and looking at where the opportunities are in ensuring that their real estate investments are aligned to their financial objectives,” he said. The problem is not limited to investors. The advisory ecosystem itself faces a structural gap, Marwadi said. There is an income parity gap between registered investment advisers and distributors of financial products. Distribution-linked incentives can create a conflict with customer interests, while fiduciary advice carries a higher standard of responsibility, he said. “If we want to solve for outcomes and if we want to solve for aligned incentives, so that advisors or fintechs that are aligned to customer outcomes flourish, we need to solve for recurring payment mechanism for earning fees that's not linked to the product manufacturer, but that's an arrangement and agreement between the investor and the advisor or the fintech platform,” he said. Marwadi also called for greater portability of financial investments. Investors should be able to move their holdings from distributors to registered investment advisers, or from regular to direct mutual fund plans, with less friction. Currently, moving from a regular to a direct mutual fund plan can result in a capital gains tax event, creating a barrier for investors who want to change their arrangement, he said. Industry needs to measure investor outcomes Mohankumar Swaminathan, Chief Product Officer, Scripbox Wealth Managers said the industry should reconsider the metrics it uses to measure the success of financial inclusion. Assets under management, the number of SIPs and other participation metrics are useful activity indicators, but they do not necessarily show whether households are becoming financially better off, he said. The industry should instead track metrics such as how many SIPs are linked to specific financial goals, whether those SIPs continue until the goal is achieved and whether investors restart SIPs after discontinuing them. “These are all activities we should measure. That is leading indicator, but also outcomes should be measured, and outcomes should be incentivized to do,” Swaminathan said. This could mark a shift from measuring how many investors are participating in the financial system to measuring whether those investors are making progress towards their financial objectives. Data portability key to financial advice Sharath Bulusu, Senior Director - Product Management, Google Pay said technology-led solutions will be essential if financial advice is to reach India’s population at scale. Even human advisers will need technology to manage larger numbers of clients effectively, he said. One of the biggest challenges today is that an individual’s financial information remains fragmented across different providers and formats. Gaps remain in the frequency, granularity and completeness of data, Bulusu said. Greater portability and interoperability could also improve competition among financial service providers. “Wherever portability comes in, wherever interoperability comes in, rent-seeking behavior disappears, and instead, what you end up getting is people compete on the value they create for the customer. They compete on innovation, and that is the need of the hour,” Bulusu said. He said greater portability could allow investors to move between advisers and providers more easily, while forcing businesses to compete on the value they provide to customers. Financial profile needs to go beyond risk appetite Marwadi said a financial advice stack should create a more comprehensive profile of an investor rather than relying only on conventional risk profiling. His approach includes factors such as financial personality, generational profile, life stage, profession, income potential, expenses, liabilities and asset allocation. The panel also discussed the growing number of first-time investors entering the formal financial system. Swaminathan said the initial enthusiasm among new investors can fade when they encounter a financial shock or lifestyle change. One of the first things investors may do when their bank balance comes under pressure is stop an ongoing SIP, he said. He argued that investors should first focus on basic financial priorities such as insurance and debt management before taking on more complex investment decisions. “Investment should be boring,” Swaminathan said. Linking investments to specific goals can also help investors overcome behavioural hurdles, he said. When an SIP is connected to a meaningful goal, investors may be less likely to discontinue it because of short-term financial pressures. AI could bring greater personalisation Artificial intelligence could add another layer of personalisation to financial advice, Bulusu said. Technology can analyse not just financial information but also an individual’s behaviour and interactions with digital platforms to understand preferences. He said people can sometimes be more candid with large language models because they may feel less judged than when speaking to another person. This could help technology better understand an individual’s preferences and financial behaviour. For investors with relatively simple financial situations, technology could potentially provide much of the required guidance. More complicated financial situations, meanwhile, may continue to require human intervention.                        Discover the latest  Business News ,  Sensex , and  Nifty  updates. There is an income parity gap between registered investment advisers and distributors of financial products. This could mark a shift from measuring how many investors are participating in the financial system to measuring whether those investors are making progress towards their financial objectives.

He said greater portability could allow investors to move between advisers and providers more easily, while forcing businesses to compete on the value they provide to customers.

Marwadi said a financial advice stack should create a more comprehensive profile of an investor rather than relying only on conventional risk profiling. His approach includes factors such as financial personality, generational profile, life stage, profession, income potential, expenses, liabilities and asset allocation.

Linking investments to specific goals can also help investors overcome behavioural hurdles, he said. When an SIP is connected to a meaningful goal, investors may be less likely to discontinue it because of short-term financial pressures.

Artificial intelligence could add another layer of personalisation to financial advice, Bulusu said.
